Without even touching the lackluster story and subpar quests: the base version of the latter game is mediocre. Particularly, fans of earlier entries in the series, especially one set in a unique fantasy world, often criticize it. While that earlier game isn't flawless, many of its issues stem from technical limitations of its time, whereas many of the latter game's faults are deliberate design choices. There are aspects the latter game gets right, but in some ways, it perfectly illustrates how making a game "more accessible" can actually detract from its overall quality by significantly simplifying certain gameplay elements that shouldn't have been simplified.

On PC, many of the latter game's annoyances can be directly attributed to developing for outdated console limitations (it remains a prime example of poor user interface design, as well as very poor memory management and harsh memory limitations, subpar dynamic draw distances and level of detail ranges, mediocre quality stock textures, poor anti-aliasing implementation, and more). The game doesn't even make real use of advanced graphics features on PC. It was never designed with 64-bit support because older consoles didn't support it, despite how much benefit it would have gained from it. Not to mention, it was hardly playable right after installation without configuration tweaks if you weren't using a controller (or it was for the first several months after release; I have no idea what it's like now). There was a lot of lazy development on the part of the studio with the latter game on PC. I've encountered a few bugs with the third installment (nothing compared to the latter game), but the overall game design and writing quality far surpasses it.

Most PC players who rave about the latter game do so because you can extensively modify it. Frankly, that's the only reason it has lasting appeal. It's somewhat ironic that one of the best modifications for it circumvents the studio's memory issues, which were a combination of the outdated engine it runs on and a low hard limit set for consoles (why this wasn't different in the PC version is beyond me).

This is coming from someone who could hardly manage 20 hours in the base version of the latter game and now has over 250 in it with modifications. I've never finished the main story in that game because, frankly, it's incredibly dull and the characters are so two-dimensional that I just don't care about any of them.

The above might have come off a bit like I'm criticizing consoles; that's not my intention. Rather, I want to illustrate that the latter game was held back by poor design decisions and the need to make significant technical compromises due to the old hardware it had to run on. There are a few compromises in the third installment from a technical perspective, but they certainly didn't simplify the gameplay in the name of "accessibility."

I'm currently writing a short story series that has similarities to a popular fantasy saga. This isn't surprising since it was the works of a well-known author that inspired me to get back to writing (fantasy writing in particular), and I have no doubt that anyone familiar with his work who read mine could find some similarities.

Having said that, there are *a lot* of differences too. For example, my story has wizards and sorcerers (one of the main characters is a sorceress), but I've built my own magic system that has no resemblance to the original author's at all. While the *feel* of my world is similar and I've tried to maintain the gritty, dark atmosphere that the original author wrote, it's still my world. It has its own politics, its own story. The main characters have their own allegiances and motivations. Yes, I've got a main character who sorta falls in love with a sorceress. Mages are often advisers in royal courts. My main character is a skilled swordsman. Overall though those are pretty generic. My main character isn't a mutant - he's an expert in a very specific type of martial combat. He doesn't fight monsters. He's often shunned because of racism, but that's because his kingdom dominated others in a war that happened 10 years prior, before his people were almost completely annihilated using magic. So while I've taken a lot of inspiration from the original series, I'm very much working on my own story.

So you want to write about monster hunters? Sure. That's a pretty generic idea and leaves a TON of room for you to do your own thing. Why are there monsters in the world? Why do monster hunters exist? Maybe they're a highly respected, elite military unit instead of mutants? That leaves you a lot more room to have them work together, introducing more characters and possible inter-character conflict, etc. And you could do that while maintaining the "feel" of the world similar to what the original author created, if you wanted to.

Frankly, the market is sparse right now; you've basically only got one quality entry in each category. I'll do a quick summary here:

*A quick note on prices: This stuff is very subject to regional pricing, some of it extremely so. Don't be surprised if you go on an online retailer and see different prices listed than what I have down here. For the most part, I've used regional pricing as a guide.*

**Under $100 Bracket**

* A budget joystick: I would consider this the bottom-of-the-barrel entry. MSRP is around $30, so you're not going to find anything cheaper. Poor design, throttles in a very awkward position. Cheaply made, few buttons. Ambidextrous. I believe this was originally made as a controller for a previous gaming console.

* A mid-range joystick: Better than the above. Much more customizable. In my opinion, an expensive stick for what you get, especially if you're in Europe and can get better options. Better throttle placement than the budget joystick. Might be worth looking into if you find most sticks uncomfortable.

* A specific model joystick: Oddball stick for the simple fact that, despite the cost and "meh" plastic build, it's got a lot going for it. Uses magnetic sensors instead of cheap components, very accurate, ambidextrous. Compatible with specific software (big, BIG plus).

* A budget 3D joystick: Cheap stick. Poor quality components. I've had calibration issues with them. Can develop spiking. Won't last near as long as better sticks; you get what you pay for.

* A budget HOTAS: Personally not a fan, as it has all the problems of a cheap joystick crammed into a HOTAS form-factor. Maybe only useful to see if you like the HOTAS setup, but keep in mind it's a $30-$50 HOTAS when "proper" HOTAS systems start at $160. **Is not** compatible with specific software, which I believe totally kills it.

**$100 - $200 Bracket**

* A specific model joystick + a throttle: In my opinion, the best budget HOTAS solution. The good-for-the-money joystick combined with the best throttle unit on the market. Makes use of specific software for the stick and another for the throttle. Gives you twist on the stick + a fully analogue thumbstick on the throttle.

* An older model joystick: Old design. Generally requires modifications to make it a decent stick. Known for throttle quadrant failures. On the plus side, the old design improved over the original means that many quality control issues don't apply to this stick. Personally, I found them *very* sloppy, poor centering requiring a large deadzone, and poor calibration. This was all on an unmodified stick though.

* A newer model joystick: Good stick on par with the money if you get one that works. Quality control is often poor, though. Issues range from button ghosting, buttons not working, sticks dead on arrival, throttle issues, and other problems. Some people have had to return multiple times before they got one that worked. Others got one that worked out of the box. Very large stick with sub-optimal button layout. Throttle unit is better in this regard.

**$300 - < $500 Bracket**

* A specific brand HOTAS: Must be bought in pieces (throttle, stick, pedals). In my opinion, the best quality HOTAS on the market. Yes, it's "plastic," but that plastic is fibre-reinforced nylon polymer. This brand builds products for industrial, agricultural, and military use. Their products last forever (20+ years, no joke). Only throttle that has an analogue thumbstick. Best control software on the market. All components have some odd ergonomics some users don't like. No twist (not a liability, in my opinion). Uses high-quality components. Modeled after the stick and throttle in a specific fighter jet. Unfortunately, very subject to regional pricing and difficult to find outside of North America. Large stick; roughly the same size as the newer model joystick but with a better button layout.

**>$500 Bracket**

* A specific model joystick: Stick licensed copy of the one in a well-known military aircraft. Very sturdy exterior build on the stick, though still uses plastic internal parts. Very heavy throw weight. In my opinion, the best looking of all the sticks. Compatible with specific software. No twist. Better suited to jet simulations than space simulations or WWII simulations, but still a good stick.

**Others**

* A specific brand: Please see [this post](http://www.reddit.com/r/EliteDangerous/comments/32npc9/hi_i_am_a_newbie_any_joystick_recomendations/cqd902p).

**My Personal Recommendations**

* Best Budget Stick: A specific model joystick.

* Best Budget HOTAS: A throttle + a specific model joystick (or two of the same joystick if all you play is a specific game).

* Best HOTAS: Full setup from a specific brand. Unless you're playing a lot of jet simulations, then probably the specific model joystick.

**What about pedals?**

If you don't have a twist stick, they're pretty much required. Even if you have a twist stick, I can't recommend pedals enough. They give you far more control and feel much more natural, not to mention you don't end up straining your wrist over longer gaming sessions.

RAM speed is arguably more important than RAM amount.

To expand a bit on how a popular open-world game’s memory management works:

The application is 32-bit, full stop. That means the game is limited to 32-bit memory address space, which means on a 64-bit system you can use a full 4GB of RAM, but no more (actually only 3, since the upper 1GB is reserved for OS space on a 32-bit process - this is true for both 32-bit and 64-bit operating systems). For the program that includes system RAM and video RAM. They're addressed from the same pool. Not actually sure about that.. virtual memory addressing is weird and partially hardware controlled. Regardless, the program can't use more than 3GB of memory.

The memory problems the game encountered before a specific memory patch have to do with how the engine allocates RAM, not necessarily physical RAM limitations in itself (basically, the engine messed up calls for more RAM causing a hard crash. The memory patch forces the game to allocate more memory on load, significantly reducing or eliminating the messy calls for more RAM).

An external enhancement tool is capable of using memory in addition to the memory allocated from the game. This is what's responsible for consuming RAM/VRAM in addition to the 4GB the game uses. So the effects from the enhancement tool aren't chewing into the program's main memory pool. The total memory in use makes sense with the memory patch + demanding enhancements.

An SSD will make a difference in load speed only, particularly when the program has to swap pages out of virtual memory and into system or video memory. A graphics card with faster RAM will be able to stream textures in and out of VRAM faster which will also lead to smooth performance.

In my experience, scripts are the things that are going to disrupt your game more than high-resolution textures. Textures will just hurt performance (up to a point.. obviously, forcing the game to load more textures into memory than your system can handle will cause problems.. but again with the memory patch this usually manifests itself in extreme slowdowns more than crashes. Hence why I'd claim faster VRAM is more beneficial).

That's fine, except it makes two assumptions: First, that the attacker is completely external to the system/infrastructure, and second that the attacker does not have physical access to the system or infrastructure.

The biggest security breaches come from insiders or insiders working in collusion with outsiders. Those are incredibly difficult threats to protect against when dealing with information that you have to have readily available. A security solution doesn't work if *nobody* can access the data. Nor does it work if you can't ensure the integrity of that data (very hard to do in a large infrastructure if your system isn't connected to anything).

There's a common principle in IT security called the 'CIA Triangle' - Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. A good security model has to be able to provide all three.

I knew about the damage system; I just didn't think it was going to port well to high complexity online play. My bet was that halfway through online development they would have to say, 'look, this damage model is too complicated, latency issues make shots not that accurate anyway, and calculating all this for the planned number of ships is killing our servers; why don't we simplify it to something more manageable instead?'

Interestingly enough, their more advanced damage system actually reduced overhead. The original model had something like 100 unique, individual damage states, each with different modeled components. Each time a ship was loaded, four completely different models had to be loaded into memory. This is the "traditional" way damage states are done.

The developers went to a component-based procedural damage system, which had the two-fold effect of increasing the fidelity of their damage modeling while decreasing the resource requirements for the physical ships (the new model uses 150MB less memory than the original, lower fidelity one).

Two other areas they wanted to improve on were the time it takes their artists to create the numerous damage states for each part of the ship and the hefty memory cost these meshes come with, which could prove to be a problem as they scale up the game. The reason the damage states are so labor-intensive is that each ship has over ten main parts, and each of these requires five damage states to represent the different levels of damage, then each of these requires up to five simplified meshes that are used when they’re further from the camera to save performance. This equates to over 200 meshes per ship!

When you examine the current damage states in the game, you’ll notice that the first two damage states tend to just contain minor dents, some burn damage, and perhaps a few panels that have been blown off exposing some internals. It’s only when you get to the 75% and 100% damage states that you start seeing major silhouette changes; however, the earlier damage states still carry the same memory cost. So their goal was to try and achieve the minor damage without having to create whole new meshes, saving both memory and artist time. To do this, they decided to record the impacts on the ship within an extra set of textures that wrap around the entire ship and then use these in the shaders to dynamically add the dents and burn in precisely the location where the ship took the damage. Ok, did some testing with a specific ship model, with the caveat that the entire series it belongs to is a little wonky, as it's mightily due for an overhaul (it's the only flyable model that hasn't had one).

I saw the behavior you're talking about with that ship. But here's the thing: It 100% makes sense based on the thruster placement on this series. The ship has particularly strong pitch moments, with a total of eight thrusters available for pitch control (positive, six negative), all but two of which are on the far extents of the ship giving you very long moments. This model can pitch and yaw faster than almost any other ship. HOWEVER: Only two of those thrusters are placed so they can effectively reduce forward velocity. This means unless you're moving exceptionally slow you're going to have far more authority to pitch than you will have ability to cancel your inertia. This is compounded by the two front thrusters -the ones that will help kill your velocity- having a very wide range of movement (eyeballing it I'd say in excess of 60 degrees). If you're maneuvering, those thrusters are going to be working overtime. This isn't an IFCS problem. This is a physical limitation of the way the ship is constructed. It's one of those things that give ships in this universe their different character.

The *second* issue you're seeing -and it exists in all ships but is very noticeable in this model, again because of the interesting thruster placement- is the way the flight control system handles translation movement. In coupled flight mode, the system will always divide your movement between commanded forward movement (throttle) and commanded translation. If you're at full throttle, the system will only allow something like 30% of your velocity vector to be translation. As you reduce throttle, that ratio goes up. So at 50% throttle, more than half of your total velocity will be dedicated to translation.

If you're using the keyboard for thrusters instead of an analog control, this makes maintaining the space equivalent of coordinated flight exceptionally difficult, because as your commanded forward speed (throttle setting) decreases (which you might do if you're trying to stay coordinated) the system is actually going to *increase* your translation vector.

A flight control computer to maintain 100% coordinated space flight, with the way the ships work in this universe, really isn't possible without drastically limiting their rotation rates or reducing their potential inertia. This model is a real offender of the issue you're talking about because its long control moments (giving it very rapid rotation) make its thrusters seem much more powerful than they actually are, especially based on their locations. The ship has always skidded around a lot, right from day one.

In theory you *could* limit rotation rates to a point where thrusters can compensate for the ship's inertia, but in many cases -especially with models like this one- those rotation rates would be exceptionally slow at anything approaching normal speeds. Thrusters in this universe simply aren't that powerful.

**TL;DR:** The behavior you're seeing actually makes sense based on the thruster placement of this model and how the flight model works in this universe.

edit:

In testing, I was able to maintain coordinated pitch at around 70-80 m/s, at about 40% pitch rate and 50% ventral thrust with stabilization off. Stabilization ON was about the same result *without* applying any thrust power. Applying thrust with stabilization ON I could peak at around 100 m/s, actually resulting in a wider -not sharper- turn. In both cases applying 100% thrust (which would happen if using keyboard control) I was unable to maintain a coordinated loop.

This testing was hardly exhaustive, as the conditions used when entering the maneuver drastically changed my results (entering from full speed/no translation, full speed/thrusters ramping up, full speed/full translation, etc), and the results would further change depending on the direction of rotation due to non-symmetrical thruster placement. But based on my understanding of the flight control system, the flight model, and this specific model, I didn't see anything that made me go "huh?".

Good sticks are expensive. Very much like comparing a cheap $12 keyboard to a $150 mechanical one. The cheap one "works," but you don't realize how poor it is until you type on the expensive mechanical one. There is a complete night-and-day difference between a cheap stick and a more expensive one.

Some of the problems you get with cheap sticks:

* Deadzone. That is, a "dead" area around the center where you get no reaction from movement of the stick. Better sticks have zero deadzone.

* Quality. Better sticks are just built better. Unlike mice, a joystick is a mechanical device that gets a lot more abuse when gaming. Cheap sticks don't stand up to abuse very well. The best quality sticks can last 15 years and still function like the day they were bought. Cheaper sticks sometimes don't even make it 6 months before they start to develop issues. Cheaper sticks sometimes even have buttons that are dead on arrival or don't work properly after a very short period of time.

* Precision. Cheap sticks have inferior internals. They're not precise. They don't calibrate well, and they'll develop 'spiking' over time (spiking is a quick and uncommanded "blip" in the stick's motion). Expensive sticks use significantly higher quality internals, and the motion on them is much smoother. This means it's easier to game with. Imagine using a mouse that would randomly move your cursor a couple of inches every now and then. That's what joystick spiking is like.

* Expensive sticks have better control software. Far too many people underestimate the usefulness of a joystick's control software. This software lets you do things like assign keymaps for programs, macros, custom sensitivity and response curves, axis reassignment or axis inversion, and depending on the software, other more complex functions. Some brands have decent software, while others are widely considered the best on the market.

* Expensive sticks have better resale value. You can probably reclaim 80-90% of what you spent on a good stick or HOTAS if it's lightly used and you decide you don't like it. I've seen 5-year-old high-quality gear go for a mere $20-$40 less than brand new stuff.

Eh, not really. A naval warship could almost always overpower a pirate vessel, which were more often than not converted merchant ships of some sort. Even when pirates captured powerfully armed ships, they'd often remove cannons. Cannons were big, heavy, expensive to arm (gunpowder was NOT a cheap commodity - this is one reason very few navies trained with live fire), and took up weight and deck space that was better dedicated to something else (like provisions, cargo, etc., or just to make a ship more seaworthy). There were of course notable exceptions but they were exceptions, not the rule.

What made piracy rampant was the social, economic, and political environment in the mid-late 17th and early 18th centuries.

Piracy started to decline because of changes in the sociopolitical landscape, such as a significant treaty which had the effect of basically ending privateering. It actually had very little to do with military technology.

The cheap one "works," but you don't realize how poor it is until you type on the expensive mechanical one. There is a complete night-and-day difference between a cheap stick and a more expensive one.

Some of the problems you get with cheap sticks:

* Deadzone. That is, a "dead" area around the center where you get no reaction from movement of the stick. Better sticks have zero deadzone.

* Quality. Better sticks are just built better. Unlike mice, a joystick is a mechanical device that gets a lot more abuse when gaming. Cheap sticks don't stand up to abuse very well. The best quality sticks can last 15 years and still function like the day they were bought. Cheaper sticks sometimes don't even make it 6 months before they start to develop issues. Cheaper sticks sometimes even have buttons that are DOA or don't work properly after a very short period of time.

* Precision. Cheap sticks have inferior internals. They're not precise. They don't calibrate well, and they'll develop 'spiking' over time (spiking is a quick and uncommanded "blip" in the stick's motion). Expensive sticks use significantly higher quality internals, and the motion on them is much smoother. This means it's easier to game with. Imagine using a mouse that would randomly move your cursor a couple of inches every now and then. That's what joystick spiking is like.

* Expensive sticks have better control software. Far too many people underestimate the usefulness of a joystick's control software. This software lets you do things like assign keymaps for programs, macros, custom sensitivity and response curves, axis reassignment or axis inversion, and depending on the software, other more complex functions. Some brands have decent software, while others are widely considered the best on the market.

* Expensive sticks have better resale value. You can probably reclaim 80-90% of what you spent on a good stick or HOTAS if it's lightly used and you decide you don't like it. I've seen 5-year-old gear go for a mere $20-$40 less than brand new stuff.

Actually, in the context of space simulations, it makes a ton of sense. This is the way nearly all classic space simulations are mapped (various well-known titles in the genre). The outlier in this regard is one particular game.

The mindset is *stick left, go left.* In that game, you have *one* dominant directional control, and that's pitch. In another popular space simulation, you have *two* dominant directional controls, and that's yaw and pitch. So you map your dominant directional controls to your primary axis. In fact, I often try and encourage new players to get out of the "bank and yank" mindset, as rolling in that game does you absolutely nothing in terms of changing direction (same with the other game, though because you really only have pitch to work with, it doesn't leave you much choice).

In terms of atmospheric flight, the exact same principle applies. In aircraft, your dominant directional controls are roll and pitch. Your dominant directional controls go on your primary control axis. Because an aircraft will go left when you roll left, the mindset of *stick left, go left* still applies.

You really have to get it out of your mind that you're flying an airplane (because you're not), and get into the mindset of what makes sense for *directional control*.

Having said that, if having roll on your third axis really bothers you, you can always remap it. Though I encourage everyone to give it a try. In my opinion, it is quite superior to yaw on your third axis.
